Life from age 4 to 16

I like hearing how someone arrived at an explanation, especially when there is more than one possibility. The hospital shift made me curious, but I know listening at a desk is very different from being responsible for a patient.

  • family: Lives with parents and a younger sibling; grandmother visits weekly.
  • finances: Stable moderate income; lengthy education would require planning.
  • geography: San Antonio, Texas.
  • cultureLanguages: English-speaking household with relatives in several states.
  • school: Public high school with biology and a supervised volunteer partnership.
  • accessOpportunities: Library sources, school experiments, and an approved hospital information-desk placement.
  • Age 4–5

    In 2014, Ari enjoyed making elaborate pretend journeys for stuffed animals and asking adults why some roads were closed. They also liked building towers, usually losing interest before putting the blocks away.

  • Age 6–7

    At six, Ari joined a recreation-center swim class and liked the routine more than the races. During 2017, a grandparent’s stories prompted questions about why different people remembered the same afternoon differently.

  • Age 8–9

    In 2018, Ari prepared a classroom animal report and changed it after finding two sources disagreed. They liked explaining the disagreement, although classmates mostly wanted to hear the unusual facts and see the pictures.

  • Age 10–11

    During 2020, Ari helped organize family video calls and learned to wait while relatives finished speaking. Online science lessons were uneven; practical classroom work later made more sense than watching demonstrations through a small screen.

  • Age 12–13

    In 2022, Ari completed a class experiment and found comparing possible explanations satisfying. By 2023, a health presentation led them to check sources carefully and ask why similar symptoms could arise for different reasons.

  • Age 14–15

    In 2025, an approved, supervised hospital information-desk shift involved directing visitors to the correct destination. Ari liked listening and explaining, while understanding that finding a department provided no experience examining, diagnosing, or treating anyone.

  • Age 16

    At sixteen in 2026, Ari is looking into Texas college science programs and what medical school and residency actually involve. A modest independent life during training seems acceptable, but they have not experienced clinical responsibility or sustained professional study.

Life now

  • enjoys: Comparing explanations · Listening · Learning biology
  • avoids: Unverified health claims · Assuming one observation settles a question
  • activities: Biology coursework · Health presentation · Supervised information-desk volunteering
  • demonstratedSkills: Checked sources · Completed a class experiment · Directed visitors clearly
  • unfamiliarActivities: Patient examination · Treatment · Clinical training demands
  • motivations: Useful work · Continuing to learn
  • ambitions: Explore college and the possible medical training sequence · They imagine modest independence and close relationships while continuing their education.
  • struggles: Uncertain about training costs and workload · Can overresearch a small assignment
  • supports: Parents · Biology teacher · Volunteer supervisor
  • practicalConstraints: Long training would need financial planning · Limited clinical exposure

Still uncertain: Would consultations remain appealing with real responsibility? · What would prolonged training feel like in daily life?

Conditional preview of the first displayed career, to test preparation and money. This is not a student choice or a correct-career answer key.

Career: Physician · family medicine

Preparation: Medical school, residency, and a Texas physician license.

  • Complete college prerequisites and an MD or DO.
  • Family medicine residency usually takes 3 years.
  • Meet Texas licensing exams, training, and eligibility requirements.

Training budget before aid: $399,818 · 8.0 study years in this reference

Still needs funding: $399,818 · loan payments $0/month · included in lifestyle: no

Annual pay before tax: $69,528 · Published paid-training example · residency

Chosen-life income range: $47,000–$60,000

Budget result: This pay covers your lifestyle. Your costs and savings fit, with money left over.

Financial assumptions: Supported wish: a modest independent life during continued study. Rent and restrained spending express that wish; exact housing, transit, food, dining, travel, entertainment, recreation, clothing and saving levels are modest single-adult reference choices, not stated budgets.

Next steps

  • An earlier activity

    I like hearing how someone arrived at an explanation, especially when there is more than one possibility. The hospital shift made me curious, but I know listening at a desk is very different from being responsible for a patient.

  • Explore a health question

    Use two reliable sources to explain a general health question. Notice whether you enjoy the science, explanation, or both. Try a supervised healthcare activity through a youth program.

  • Map college, medical school, and residency

    Compare college prerequisites, four-year medical training, and family medicine residency. Budget each stage separately; no college major guarantees medical school admission.

  • Ask about a normal day in family medicine

    Ask a physician and a resident about patient contact, paperwork, training hours, and what they wish they knew in high school.
